newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's opposition heartland drifts away.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's opposition heartland drifts away.

text.p: Zaire's opposition heartland and diamond mining Kasai region is drifting steadily away from central authority despite no apparent separatist sentiment.
Kasai even has its own currency zone since radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi told his supporters not to accept a new Zairean currency introduced in 1993.
When Tshisekedi repeated his claim to be prime minister during a visit to France last week, the value of the old Zaire currency strengthened from 16 million to the dollar to 15 million to the dollar.

The figures may appear almost comical but Kasai's commitment to sticking with its own currency has preserved it from the hyperinflation of the rest of the chaotic state -- there is no government to print money when it needs to spend and the exchange rate has not moved significantly for three years.
And buttressed by revenues from diamond mining the regional capital Mbuji-Mayi is almost entirely self-sufficient.
The state within a state is far removed from the latest crisis that has spread into the rest of the chaotic nation with an advance by Tutsi-led rebels in the eastern border region.
In the local market, designer suits and sophisticated electronic goods flown in via Mbuji-Mayi's tiny airport crowd rickety wooden tables piled with local foodstuffs.

Although the majority state-owned industrial diamond mining company MIBA has to send its receipts back to Kinshasa, those from the artisanal pits that pepper the nearby river beds make a far greater contribution to the local economy.
In the absence of any assistance from Kinshasa, Kasaians have turned to themselves to carry out the projects that in another country would be the job of the central government.

"We have waited for too long for assistance from rulers who have no interest in this region and if anything is going to be done here we have to organise to do it amongst ourselves," said local merchant Kalonje wa Tshimanga, chairman of the Mbuji-Mayi business association.

The group has already paid for work to halt erosion that threatened to cut Mbuji-Mayi in two and now plans its most ambitious project yet, a $13.6 million hydroelectric dam that would make the city self-sufficient in electricity.
"The studies have all been carried out and now it is a matter of collecting the funds together and beginning the project," said Kalonje.
Help has also been given to resettle Kasaians driven from neighbouring Shaba in 1993, after Kasaians were accused of taking the best jobs in the copper and cobalt mining region.
Unlike in Shaba, where separatist feeling is barely hidden, there is no serious move to sever Kasai from the rest of the huge state.
"Kasai is part of Zaire and will remain part of it, and if the powers that be try to divide us it is because of our support for Tshisekedi," said student activist Moussa Mulamba.
"When he returns as prime minister and is given a chance to work then everyone in Zaire will see what we have been able to do here repeated across the country."
Tens of thousands of Tshisekedi's supporters lined the streets of Kinshasa on Thursday to welcome him home after a trip to Europe.
He said his symbolic handshake in France with president Mobutu Sese Seko marked the start of national reconciliation.

Tshisekedi's two terms as prime minister during almost seven years of transition to civil rule were characterised by personal conflict between himself and the president and did little to unscramble the chaos that dogs Zaire.
Removed by Mobutu in 1993, Tshisekedi still proclaims himself prime minister to his faithful in Kasai and in Kinshasa and rejects the election by parliament of centrist Kengo wa Dondo in 1994.
